title: Memory System
markdown:
The Executive's durable memory is an episodic SQLite store at `./episodic_memory.db`, managed by `openexecutive.memory.episodic`. It holds four tables:

- `decisions` — choices made, with `domain`, `summary`, `rationale`, `outcome`, and `tags`.
- `initiatives` — tracked efforts with a `status` and `summary` (idempotent upserts).
- `advice_given` — query/advice pairs per domain.
- `scheduled_actions` — a dispatch queue, treated separately from recall memory.

### What gets extracted, and when

`episodic.extract_and_store` runs after a turn and asks a utility-fast model for decisions, initiatives and advice. Every candidate must carry a `user_commitment_quote` that appears verbatim in the principal's own message (`_is_valid_user_commitment`) — the model has repeatedly tried to log the Executive's *recommendations* as the user's commitments, and that quote is the hard gate against it.

A turn reaches the extractor only if the **user's** message clears `MIN_USER_CHARS_FOR_EXTRACTION`. This was a combined user+assistant floor, and on a live tenant it selected almost exactly the wrong turns: 9 of 16 exchanges were blocked, and the 9 held every instruction the principal gave, while the 7 admitted were long analytical exchanges with no commitment in them. The extractor ran 13 times and stored nothing. Decisive instructions are short ("Correct it there", "Don't track this"); the analysis around them is long, so a floor that scales with the Executive's verbosity discards exactly what it is meant to capture. The floor now measures only the user's side — the one place a commitment, and an acceptable quote, can come from.

Each pass writes a `memory_extraction` audit row: how many items the model proposed, how many were stored, and the reason each drop was rejected. Without it, "the model found nothing" and "the model found things and every one was rejected" are indistinguishable from outside the database — which is why the failure above survived undetected and took a SQLite session on the tenant to find. A `proposed>0, stored=0` streak is the signal to watch.

### Session scoping

`decisions` and `advice_given` rows carry a `session_id`, so per-thread channels (Discord, Telegram) can pull just-this-thread history without leaking cross-conversation context. A null `session_id` falls back to a global view.

### Surfacing

`openexecutive.memory.episodic.format_for_prompt` renders recent decisions and initiatives into a compact `<past_decisions>` block injected into the user turn — alongside `<retrieved_context>` and peer memory — never into a cached system block.

The chat route also injects a `<briefing>` block into the same user turn: a compact digest of the current open (unread) alerts, built by `openexecutive.briefing.context.format_open_alerts_for_prompt` (company-wide, `status="unread"`, mirroring `/today`). This is what lets the Executive discuss a briefing item the principal clicked or named on `/today` (e.g. "Gulf Coast Port Cyberattack"). It is resolved in parallel with the other context fetches, omitted when there are no open alerts, and never placed in a cached system block.

### System of record

SQL is the system of record; the peer-memory service is a recall layer mirrored from it, not a replacement. When `store_decision` / `store_initiative` / `store_advice` insert a row whose `department` is non-empty and not `"general"`, the row is mirrored as a kind-tagged note into that department's peer via `append_department_note`. The mirror fires only after a successful INSERT, is fire-and-forget, and never rolls back the SQL row on peer-memory failure. `scheduled_actions` is never mirrored — it is a queue, not memory.
